utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, if I could remind you of the affirmation you took at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, we arrived yesterday at the position where you had arrived back in Kosovo and you had arrived in Klecka itself and you indicated that the date was around about the 20th of March of 1998. Now, that's the position and the question I want to ask you is: What was the situation like in Klecka when you got there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After our arrival in Klecke, as I said earlier I went to the family of my nephew's. Klecka is a small village. It has about 20 households. We didn't see anything particular when we arrived. As I said, we just went and settled down with that family. And at that moment, nothing struck us with the exception of the fact that people started to get worried and interested in recent developments which has occurred in Drenica. We heard various comments on that by people who spoke about those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It is clear from yesterday that you had not been ordered to go to Klecka, you chose to go there for the reasons you gave. What were you intending to do, having arrived there? What did you think you could do?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need some time to give you an answer, for you to understand the way we operated then. We didn't have any orders and for your information it was outside normal practice for someone to give orders to another person to go from one place to another. The way the KLA operated at that time in Drenica or in other places was an exclusively guerrilla warfare, and as such it was a quite reasonable, normal thing for anyone or a group of people to operate in the region they knew better, in the place they could find shelter, where they could receive assistance by the local population. So from the time of my return from Switzerland, I was determined to go back to my municipality, but if the circumstances were such that they required us to act differently, we would do that. At that time we believed that Serbia would continue with military operations in other villages of Drenica. And if situation was similar to that of Likoshan and Qirez, of course we would help them, the guerrilla units of the KLA, which at that time were operating in the Drenica region. But since the Serbian forces had encircled Drenica, but they were not organising any further military operations, there was a kind of provisional calm situation. I deemed it inappropriate to remain in the village I described to you yesterday. Furthermore, as I said earlier, it was necessary to expand the operation of the KLA in other areas. That's what -- these were the reasons that accounted for my decision to go back to the place, that is to Klecke. Our activity in Klecke was clear to us. I remember before going to Klecke in a talk we had with Rexhep and Hashim, we touched on some general issues, one of them being that during the actions or operations that might be undertaken by us as a guerrilla unit in Malisheve we should be careful not to [Realtime transcript read in error: "careful to"] attack the Serbian army or attack only the Serbian police. Because the Serbian army at that time was not involved in the violence and repression exerted against the people. And on the other hand, in this way we believed we would enable the recruits of the Serbian army to realise that the situation in Kosova was such that they should desert the Yugoslav Army. These were some topics, some suggestions we thrashed out amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just one moment. It's just that I think the transcript may have left a word out. I thought I heard you say "when dealing with guerrilla operations ... should be careful not to attack the Serbian army or attack only the Serbian police." As we have it written, the word "not" is omitted. I'm sorry to interrupt. Is that what you said, "not to attack"?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask that is borne in mind for the final transcript. It's at line 6 -- I'm sorry, is it 8? Page 3, yes, page 3, line 6, not to attack. These were the topics that you discussed. The question I want to ask of course is a rather obvious one. Was there already any kind of unit or gathering or group of KLA members in Klecka when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely not. We were the first armed people as members of the KLA to arrive in that territory, the three of us. Indeed at that time I thought we were the first in Malisheve municipality for that matter. As the first members of the KLA. But as events later showed there had been other people in profound illegality, as the nature of our operations were at that time. If you allow me, I would like to touch on another issue which I think is important. It has to do with the topics we discussed with Rexhep. In addition to the two I mentioned earlier, there was another topic. At that time we were eager to hear from Rexhep as to what to do, how to act, when we arrived there. The guerrilla operations which we might undertake after our settlement in Malisheve, we should be careful not to undertake any military operations during the day at first; and second, we should not undertake any guerrilla actions in places where we could -- might endanger the lives of the civilian population. There were two possibilities for us to attack, either police stations or patrols along the streets, but always in late evening hours where the risk at civilians would be minimum or it wouldn't be existent at all. Because under that situation, when dark fell civilians didn't go out usually. Regarding our stay in Klecke, as I said, there were only the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And could you just remind us, who are the three, beside yourself, obviously, who are the people you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, it was -- besides myself it was myself, Haxhi Shala, and Ismet Jashari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to move forward a little in time. You've arrived towards the end of March. And at the end of March now into April of 1998, what in fact did you personally set about doing? You had weapons. I'll ask you this: Did you have a uniform then?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, what did you exactly start doing at the end of March, April, bearing in mind the nature of what you had in mind, the various points you discussed earlier? What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we settled down in Klecke, we rested for about a week. The people who used to go out during the day sounded out the situation on the ground and the movements of the Serb forces, to see where they were going, how many of them were moving. After getting some general information, we started to operate as became normal in other parts where the KLA had been active. That is, we started to move at night to go to the villages of Malisheve to be -- to make known our presence in the region. That was the only way for us to make ourselves present before the eyes of the inhabitants, for them to see that the KLA would be present also in the villages of Malisheve. That was one of the forms, to show our presence in that -- those villages in that region. Usually we would go out in the evening. We patrolled the streets, stopped some vehicles, then visited some villages. We entered some shops or cafes -- coffees [as interpreted], just to show that we were present in that region. That was more or less what our activity consisted of in the beginning. Then gradually we started to establish contacts with some of my former student friends, people I used to know from the past, because one of the duties that every guerrilla unit has was normally to recruit new forces. That was our purpose, to expand the ranks of the KLA, and it was part of our activity as well, establishment of contacts with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to follow through with a couple of matters on that. Just before I do, did your family, any members of your family, know that you were back in the Klecka region, other than the nephews with whom you were staying in Klecka itself? For example, did your wife, your father, mother know you were back?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one knew about my presence. Before Malisheve fell under the control of the KLA, none of the members of my family knew before that time. This happened, if I'm not wrong, after two months of my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, this -- the two questions I want to ask you about in relation to this early activity. You mentioned you went out to the villages of Malisheve. I think it's quite important, if you can, going back to that large map that you were using yesterday, the large-scale map, if you can indicate the villages -- the actual villages you went to as your area of activity at this time, and if you could do it on that large map, please.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our trips were made at random, that is just to make our presence known. We went to most of the villages of Malisheve municipality without any kind of order, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And again, if you could use a different colour, it would help so they don't get confused, one you haven't used so far.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Malisheve is situated here. It has about 50 villages. Of course we didn't visit every one of them. Our presence was mostly here in the -- in those villages. We kept away from Maline [as interpreted] village, from my native village because we didn't want people to recognise us. Mostly our movements were in this part, in this area, in Banje, Bellanice, Revasari [phoen], Dragobil, Carralluke, Goriq, Pagarushe, and so on. Bajrak, all these villages. Temeqine, Guqat [phoen], Terpeze, Lladrovc, and so on. We passed through most of the villages in the territory of Malisheve. This map doesn't show Malisheve municipality. You probably have a map that shows the borders of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: That was going to be the next question, interestingly. So while you're -- sorry. I'll just pause while you -- that was going to be the next question, the question of the municipalities. And at this time was Malisheve recognised as a particular -- either as a commune or as a municipality or what? And then we'll come to the map.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Events in 1990, just for your information, Malisheve as a municipality was ethnically -- almost ethnically pure, that is inhabited mostly by Albanians. It was declared a commune or a municipality in 1986. After the changes made by the Serb power, government, they deprived it of the status of municipality. But all the political activity and the parallel institutions of Albanians were done in Malisheve because they considered it as a municipality even though its status was changed. And this is how we acted, considering it as such. In 2000, after the war, it was made again, officially made a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, for these purposes, if you could -- you may need some help. The political map and the point you've just made is underneath one of the two maps there. I think the one on the left. It's underneath that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a map that looks like this that you should have, multi-coloured, and if you could just -- it's a very simple, straightforward point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You could indicate on the political map. It's a map, we make clear, that is produced after the war. You can then just point out where Malisheve is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Malisheve lies here, in this territory. It is more or less in the centre of Kosovo. As you can see, it has -- it borders with Raso [phoen] village, with Ostrazup village, with the part -- in the part with -- bordering Suva Reka there is Pagarushe village. In the part where there is a road that leads to Gllogoc or Drenoc, there is Terpeze village. On the side of Lipjan there is the Klecke village. So it borders with Lipjan, Rahovec, Kline, and Drenoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If you can hear the question without putting -- it appears on the map that Lapusnik does not fall within the municipality of Malisheve. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. Lapusnik has never been part of Malisheve municipality; it's been part of Drenoc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It's on the same point. Could we have, please, Prosecution Exhibit P1, map 4, please. P1, map 4. It could be on the ELMO. It might be easier, I don't know. I think everybody's got copies of this. Could it just be put on the ELMO? I'm very grateful. Once it's aligned on the ELMO -- I'm just watching to see it come up on the screen -- that's it. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, with a pointer, if you have one there, something you can point with on there, we can see that as far as this map is concerned Malisheve as a municipality is a not actually marked there. Is that correct? But we have another municipality marked in white in that region.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is a map that mirrors the administrative border according to the Serb officials. From this map you can see that Malisheve and the villages that it comprised are scattered amongst other municipalities. As I said yesterday, the village of Banje until late was part of Suva Reka municipality. When Malisheve became a municipality, a number of villages joined it, villages that until that time belonged to Suhareke municipality, Rahovec municipality, Kline municipality, and Lipjan municipality, as well as Gllogoc municipality. And these villages build up the Malisheve municipality. When the status of Malisheve as a municipality was removed, these villages were again given back to the former municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to go back to your activities, visiting villages of Malisheve as you knew it. Again, it's an obvious question: During this time, did you visit the village of Lapusnik at all?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the geographical position of Lapusnik at that time was dangerous because there was constantly movement of Serb forces. I would like to mention a fact here. Sometime in April while we were going to Likovc from Klecka, somewhere between the villages of Orlat and Gjurgjice while passing by the main road we were ambushed by the Serb forces. And Ismet Jashari was wounded on this occasion. At that time this part was completely under the control of Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So you indicated you went to villages in Malisheve - you've already named them - on a random basis. How did you choose which villages you would go to in this period?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, one of the main goals of the guerrilla units at that time and my personal goals was to visit the villages in order to show our presence in those villages and contact people who could help us or join the ranks of the KLA. The first choice for us was always the village that we knew best, which territory we knew best, or a village where I had someone that I knew from before and wanted to establish contact with that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: What was the response from the villagers in the villages you've told us you went to?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During our visits at nighttime, we were limited in meeting people. We could mostly meet four or five people, depending on the village that we visited. For example, there are villages when -- where young men stay until late at night in the village cafeterias or tea shops, and we had the opportunity to meet these people in these locations. But on the other side you had villages where you could not meet anyone, where it happened that some people went to visit their in-laws or friends in certain villages, we stopped them in order to make our presence known to them. This was our main aim, main goal. We didn't have any other goal. I would like to add that throughout the time, we were masked and we did not stay for a long time in one village. We would maximally stay for 15 minutes, 20 minutes, and leave the village. People that we met received us extremely well. They were extremely happy to have the opportunity to meet a KLA member. At that time, people were still suspicious whether there was or there was not a KLA. This was a topic often debated amongst the mass. They were in a dilemma. People were in a dilemma, whether we were Serbs or Albanians, and the policy in Pristina had helped for this confusion to arise. But however, these people were very glad when they would meet with KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, at each stage -- I'm going to ask you the same question in view of the way the case is presented against you. During this period, were you receiving instructions or orders from anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. We were three and then four or five joined us. Our goal was very clear. There wasn't the possibility for communication; it was very difficult. In order to get in touch with someone, you had to walk for hours to Likovc. And in addition, there was nothing particular to be communicated at that time, let alone orders. The guerrilla way of combat requires this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If people wanted to join, how were they going to go about it? Was there some plan or programme of how they should form a KLA unit or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. group?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak on my behalf here. Every group, every individual who dealt with the recruitment applied his own methods. But generally, the principle was only to those trusted, and those who you knew from before, only to recruit them. Because at that time the number was limited and the KLA was not interested in increasing the manpower in terms of a figure, because at that time we didn't have sufficient weapons and we didn't have any particular plan except for those guerrilla attacks. But in cases when there was armament and when there were people that we trusted, this was enough. And they became part of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And if a group or a unit was formed, who decided who might be -- lead that group in a particular village or area?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are always speaking and referring to a period of very high secrecy. And from this point of view, I will try to explain my own experience before the Honoured Judges. For example, in my municipality I contacted a person whom I knew from before, whom I trusted, and I spoke to this person because this was important for the KLA, for the liberation war, for the engagement in the KLA. And this person, if he expressed his wish and will to become a KLA member, he could from that moment start recruiting other people himself. And this is the logic behind the guerrilla way of warfare. I would recruit one person, then that person would recruit someone else, and so on and so forth. At that time, I didn't know any other person whom this person could recruit because that person could fall in the hands of the Serb authorities and could put in danger other people. So this was a responsibility of my friend, to choose who he was going to work with. If he made a bad choice, a wrong choice, the consequences were his, not ours; he suffered the consequences. And this was a way of surviving at that time of the KLA members and of the KLA guerrilla units. We were acting in illegality. We paid attention to those who could move freely during the day. Freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did this situation that you've just described, did this persist throughout the whole of April, or by the end of April had something else happened?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This situation in Malisheve community -- municipality continued until around 15th, 16th, or 29th of May. However, things began to change after the Lapusnik gorge was taken. Things began to change as of 9th of May, but definitely things changed by the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to deal with those changes, and I'll start obviously -- you've mentioned the 9th of May. I'd like you to describe in your own words what happened around and about the 9th of May as far as you're concerned.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like to mention an event that directly links with the 9th of May. I think this occurred on 29th of April. Maybe I am not quite exact with the date, but it's around this date. On this date, Rexhep Selimi, together with a friend, he passed by our terrain. He came to the Malisheve municipality and he visited me. We discussed the developments, the situation, the accurate situation in Malisheve municipality, in those villages that we had seen. And he gave me two radios, very basic radios, but very efficient for us at that time. They could only work on one channel. Simply, it was a radio that here in the west people can buy in ordinary supermarkets. On the 9th of May, we were at our base in Klecke. Until that time, we had never moved during the day and we never moved without masks. On the 9th of May, we heard some noise on the radio, some voices of KLA members who were communicating amongst them. Someone was looking for assistance, someone was explaining the situation, the developments. One was telling the other, Don't shoot because there are civilians. And from this dialogue, which was unintelligible due to the reception, I decided to go to a place where the reception was better and where I could hear the conversation clearly, just to find out what was going on. Together with four friends who happened to be there at that time and with a vehicle, we went up to the Berisa Mountains. And from there we could see - because it is possible to see from there - we could see several Serb vehicles, several Serbian policemen who was -- who were hiding behind a civilian bus. They were using this civilian bus as a shield in order to approach the KLA forces that were at Gjurgjice village. This village is situated next to Orlate village. And from the place where we were, this could be clearly seen. We could also hear well the unit that was nearby there and that could see clearly what was going on; however, the Serbian police unit could not communicate with the other police unit. And with our radio, actually, we helped them to communicate with the other unit to use the waves. We served as a kind of a bridge between the two units. As we followed these developments, on the other side of the asphalt road, on the Gjurgjice side in the direction of Orlate and up to Lapusnik pass, there was a concentration of Serb forces who were fighting and attacking KLA members in the other side of the villages. For example, if we go from Pristina to Peja, this is on the right side of the main road. As we saw these developments, we saw that a police unit, a Serb police unit, was positioned in one place, on the other side of the asphalt road as seen from the Berisa Mountains. And from this position of an extremely high strategic importance, they were firing at the other side of the road. We had gone there in order to observe the terrain. We were five or six. And on the spot, we decided to help. The five of us set off for the main road, wanted to go down to the main road at Lapusnik village, and we left one of us at the location we were before. We gave him a radio so that he could be in contact with the other units in order to avoid any possible misunderstandings that could lead to killing between KLA units, and also to make it possible for him to call other friends who were at the base as assistance. We went down the main road close to the point where our friends were being attacked. We dispersed at 5 or 10 metres of each other, just to create an impression that we were greater in numbers. We opened fire. Fortunately we shot at a Serbian Pinzgauer who was most probably loaded with ammunition. And as a result, this Pinzgauer exploded, and I think this is the reason that the Serbs left that point in panic and immediately. The withdrawal started in other parts as well from Gjurgjice and other villages. There was panic amongst the policemen. Some of them withdrew in the direction of Drenica, and the other in the direction of Komorane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I just want to ask you this question at this time: By what name were you known at this period, May the 9th?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was known by the pseudonym Daja. However, if you allow me, I would like to say that when we received the radio, at that time Rexhep Selimi had some suggestions regarding the code that was to be given because you cannot speak on a radio without a coded name. He made some suggestions, I made some suggestions. But my suggestion was not accepted. It was a name of an individual. During my stay in Prishtine, I was for some time known as Arbeni, I used the pseudonym Arbeni. And I proposed to Rexh to be called Beni. But he said, No, this doesn't sound properly on a radio. And he suggested that I should use the coded name of Celiku. So I was Celiku 1, and Celiku 2 was Kumanova because both of us had the radios. The pseudonym that I was known by amongst the soldiers was Daja. Later on when we started to communicate through radios with other units, of course we communicated as Celiku 1 unit and Celiku 2 unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Had you played any part in organising other groups than the one you were associated with?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So take the Celiku 2 unit. Did you know at that time who was in that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was no Celiku 2. We were three, four people. We had two radios. I kept one, Ismet kept the other, Rexhe sometimes, until we were together, the four of us. When one of us went out to the grassroots, the other one was Celiku 2. When there were two of us in the grounds, I was Celiku 1 and he was Celiku 2 at that time we were together. It was later that Celiku 2 was formed; it was at the end of May/beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, I'm come to the end of May in a moment. Can we meanwhile deal with what happened between May the 9th when the Serbs, in panic, dispersed and left the area, the immediately area, and the end of May. What happened after May the 9th?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us that was a guerrilla action. After successfully completing that action - because it was a successful one, we drove back the Serbian forces - we contacted some units of the KLA in that part. We talked to them, and we turned back to Klecke. Because we thought that we did the work for what we went. We had carried out a military action. We were successful, and then we would go back to our base. There were other members of the KLA from other regions and parts who happened to be there by accident, by chance, when passing from their place to Drenice or from Drenice to their respective places. So they also helped. The action was over and we returned immediately to Klecke -- maybe not immediately but one or two hours afterwards. I know there was a BBC reporter who was there and shot the Pinzgauer, and then we returned to Klecke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And in the days and weeks that followed, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would allow me, I would like to explain in a little more detail the situation we found in Lapusnik because I think it's of importance for Your Honours to know, to inform them of my experience. When we arrived in Lapusnik, we were five people. People, the civilians started to shoot at us, not knowing who we were. There was a confusion. After the departure of the Serbian forces, we met a group of soldiers -- I'm saying soldiers now because then they were a group of young men dressed in civilian clothes without any distinctive sign as being KLA members. Then we got to know them later. They were led by Ymer Alushani, a people's hero. His pseudonym was Voglushi. They were civilians who had participated in fighting along the Gjurgjice-Lapusnik main road. After this meeting, during which we got to know each other, we didn't know who they were, as I said, there was a confusion so we had to clarify it. They told us that there was a unit called Zjarri. I'm not so sure about the name - that was directly linked with Likovc and operated in Komorane area for a time. They heard the shots in Lapusnik gorge and they came to the rescue. It was like us who heard the shots and came to this place to help them. After this contact we returned to Klecke. That night, Fehmi Lladrovci, with his wife, came to Klecke. They were coming I think from Drenoc village of Sadik village. Fehmi had heard about the developments at Lapusnik gorge and on the next day he went there to see for himself. When he went there Ymer Alushani came to Klecke along with two civilians. He told us the civilians were afraid; they wanted us to go to the village, lest the Serbian forces returned. Fehmi Lladrovci knew the terrain very well and he had great authority. He came from that municipality. He talked with the villagers and the members -- Ymer's group, and with us in Klecke, telling us that we must do something to form a group or a unit, to station that unit in that place, in Lapusnik. So people went there voluntarily. I did not have enough soldiers to send to Lapusnik. There were few of us, and we were interested in operating in Malisheve municipality. Isak Musliu happened to be there at that moment. Luani too. Two young men from Drenoc village, two in-laws of Fehmi Lladrovci, and a boy from Lubizhde village, a young man who had come to stay there for some time until they found accommodation in their own area. They wanted to stay with us for three, four days. These people of their own free will joined that group, and so it happened that a group of KLA members were stationed in that part of the Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to carefully ask you about this aspect. First of all, Isak Musliu, did you know him before that time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Isak Musliu for the first time sometime in April when I went for a visit in Likovc. I had gone there to fetch some clothes for us being in Klecke and to see how my friends were doing. I hadn't seen them for quite some time. And the only place you could go out during the day was Likovc. Sometimes you just felt the urge to go out during the day, and so it was that we went to Likovc. There I met some friends from Drenice. I think Rexhep Selimi was the one who told me that there are some young men from Shtime and Lipjan municipalities who want to pass over to that territory and if you could help them. I told him, yes, we had a vehicle, a car, with which we could help them and they could continue on from foot. On my way back to Likovc when I came from Klecke, Isak and Luan travelled with me. That was our first meeting. I knew that his pseudonym then was Lumi [as interpreted]. Luani had the same pseudonym even then. They were from Shtime and Lipjan municipality. I didn't know where they were from and they too didn't know who I was, where I was from, because that was the rule then. They came to Klecke, stayed there overnight. And during the next day, because as I said we used to travel only at night. And in the evening, both of them went to their respective municipalities. On the way, I heard that they had left some of their friends who had come with them from Germany in Likovc. Until they went to the municipalities, they were going to find shelter for them. First they had to go to the grassroots to see how the situation was like, find the places to accommodate them, then go back and bring their friends with them to start their activity. As I said, they travelled next day in the evening for their respective destinations. I think it was some time -- one or two weeks later they came again. Yes, it was after two weeks. I think they came back, stayed again overnight. It was a long journey. It took them five or six hours to come to Klecke from the places they were staying. They stayed in Klecke, rested during the day because they couldn't travel during the day, and in the evening they went to Likovc. Now they didn't need any escort because they knew the way. They were familiar with the terrain now. So when they returned they came -- returned with two or three other soldiers whom they had gone to fetch to go to their respective municipalities. When they had returned from Likovc to continue to Shtime, it was then that the event of 9th of May happened and that they -- they happened to stay in Klecke, when the event of 9th of May occurred. After that development, then things changed and they changed their orientation as well. I must tell you that at that time in Shtime and Lipjan municipalities - in Lipjan and Shtime especially because the -- these municipalities were -- had mixed population - there was very tight control by the Serb forces, so the movements were very restricted and you had to be very, very careful in what you did. And it was almost impossible to do anything there. So they had seen that it was impossible -- almost impossible to act. They had come to fight for Kosova. And as I said, we are willing to render our contribution to the country, wherever we are told to go. So Isak with two or three others decided of their own free will to remain at Lapusnik gorge with the other group of soldiers that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, the question that I was going to ask you -- touched on there it's this: Did you at any time at this stage at all order Isak Musliu to do anything, or Luan, for that matter, to do anything? Were you ordering people at this moment?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, and I'm telling you again, Isak and Luan were my guests, if you like. They were at my base and not more than that. People like Isak, hundreds of them passed through that base then and later. They came there, they rested, and they went -- continued with their trip to go to their destination. This was kind of rule. We always helped people, fed them, assisted them, took paths from one place to another. That was it. That was my second meeting with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: After that did you have occasion to go to Lapusnik or the area of Lapusnik again, that is in May?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The battle, I think it was on the 17th. We went there but the Serb attack was not that serious, so we returned. We went there to help them, but there was no need for that, so we came back. Then I went again to take part in the battle of 21st of May. I'm not certain about the date. I also visited -- visited on other occasions. I have gone there to see how they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm only dealing with May at the moment. I know it's difficult because it's a long time ago. Can you give us any idea of how many times you may have gone to Lapusnik in May?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think two or three times. I'm certain about these two battles I mentioned. Maybe I have been there another time for a visit, but I'm not entirely sure about the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you a direct question in relation to Lapusnik. Did you at any time in May participate in the organisation of a prison camp in that area?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about anything else that is relevant in May. Were there other developments in other parts of Malisheve? Lapusnik you've indicated wasn't part of Malisheve. Were there other developments so far as the KLA were concerned during this time that you feel is important?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had never imagined what the significance of the Lapusnik gorge Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would be for the KLA. For us it was just another battle, but as events showed, the action, the operation in the Lapusnik gorge was a turning -- a positive turning point for us regarding the further development of the KLA and events in general. It would assume such a significant importance that we never reckoned with before. If I'm not wrong, I think that after the deployment of forces in this gorge, operations started to block the other part of the road from Kline to Kijeve. Some of the KLA units have blocked the road to prevent the Serbian forces from penetrating and hitting them on the back. And then things continued along this line. Units which -- of the KLA until now which had been underground, illegal, quite suddenly came out in the open. So units started to appear on a daily basis. So we realised that it was not only we, that is one or two groups, that were operating in Malisheve, but we saw that there had been other people doing the same thing parallel with us. So we saw the appearance of various units in different villages of Malisheve municipality. And then the organisation of units started within the villages themselves. If I am not mistaken, I think it was on the 29th of May that other roads that lead towards Malisheve started to be blocked. For example, from what had happened on Llozice road towards Kijeve or Kline, that went on in Bubavec. That is another village that leads towards Malisheve. Kijeve is a village with mixed population. It was the only place in that area where there was deployment of Serbian police forces. There was a police station there. So the KLA unit blocked the way coming from Malisheve. The same happened in Rahovec. A unit of the KLA had blocked the way leading to Malisheve, and also the way coming from Rahovec to Malisheve. The same thing happened in Suhareke from Dulje to Malisheve in Temeqine village and the road to Malisheve. From Temeqine the units merged in Bllace. So we come to a situation where Malisheve falls entirely under the control of the KLA, is regarded as a free zone. And this marks a change, a definite change, heralds new phase of developments of the KLA and in Kosova in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, this new phase, I just want to ask you this: Were you in Klecka coordinating this whole exercise in which roads gradually became blocked by particular units? Were you coordinating that? Were you coordinating the units for other purposes as well?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in these developments that I mentioned. These were developments that were unfurling as of their own. When we realised that the situation was the one that I described, I had my own reservations regarding such developments because I was worried about the eventual outcomes of such developments, the outcomes of such euphoria that started to prevail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: What was your worry? What was your concern?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, Malisheve and its villages, Malisheve as a centre, it didn't have any administration, any Serb police. It was kind of ignored by the Serb government. It was outside their interest. Malisheve was controlled by the police station of Suhareke and Rahovec. So placing it under our control, that didn't come about as a result of military actions, as the case was with the Lapusnik gorge. There we had a military action. Or in Kline. The roads around Malisheve that I mentioned, that didn't come about, the blocking of the roads, didn't come about as a result of military operations which led to the liberation of this area. We saw that part of the road was blocked and we went there to block another. We just copied one another. Out of their own free will to come out before the eyes of the public because they were tired of being in -- underground for a long time. The KLA units undertook such actions by blocking roads or forming points. So this situation found the KLA unprepared to deal with it. For the people, it was good news, it was a euphoric situation. The citizens at that time didn't know the significance of that. They were just enthralled by the euphoria of freedom. For the first time they felt safe because they knew that Serbian police couldn't pass through Malisheve without having to fight with the KLA forces. This euphoria spread all over Kosova, and I may say that there are hundreds and thousands of people from various regions, various cities of Kosova who came to Malisheve, as they said, to breathe the freedom -- the air of freedom and to see from close up the members of the KLA. It was a sudden development for the citizens of Malisheve itself, who didn't know until then who the members of the KLA were, who those individuals that came out at night were. And on a fine morning, they realised that their own children, too, were members of the KLA, something which they didn't know until then. They thought that those people were roaming the streets of Malisheve were from Drenice. When we took off our masks and they could find -- some of them could find their sons, their brothers, their nephews, their in-laws, it was a revelation for them. But it was a revelation for ourselves too, as members of the KLA, because we too didn't know that so much work had been done to recruit people. Because we saw that the emergence of several units at once. But on the other hand, such a euphoria led to the joining of the KLA by thousands of people who knew where to turn now. It was no longer the time of conspiracy. It was no longer the time when they didn't know where the base of the KLA were. Now they knew. And so they knew who they were whom they were going to meet because now we were -- they realised we were people from the same region, people they knew. So these were the developments that occurred and which I considered as a new phase of the development that would follow later. And this assumed the features of a popular uprising, as I said earlier on in my address from a guerrilla organisation with limited ambitions, with very restricted possibilities, suddenly the KLA finds itself in entirely new circumstances which I personally never believed would be the case without four or five years. But things evolved more quickly than we thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: A quick question before the break. Again, I'm concentrating at the moment the stage we've reached, which is towards the end of May. At that time with the emergence of the units in the way you've described, was there any structure to the KLA, command structure in the KLA at that time that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides what was public knowledge, that we knew of, there was a General Staff, general headquarters, central staff it was called then. And the people that I mentioned earlier were introducing themselves as members of the general headquarters. But when they -- it might be that they were members, but it might be that they were not members of the headquarters -- of the general headquarters. The only mechanism was this, the general headquarters, because at that time everything was done on the basis of friendly relations. After the developments of the 29th of May, we embarked on a new phase and measures and organisations -- organisation, too, were done differently. But until then, there was only the general headquarters and the guerrilla units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mansfield. We will resume at 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your last answer involved indicating that as far as you were concerned towards the end of May, the only structure you were aware of in relation to the KLA was the existence of the general headquarters or central staff, as they were known, and the units. One more question on that. So far as the general staff or central staff was concerned, were you aware where they were located?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take into consideration the illegal nature of the guerrilla warfare, you can imagine how and in what circumstances a central staff could exist. At that time, we could maintain contacts with one representative of the central staff. At that time, we could mostly meet in the terrain with Rexhep Selimi and Sokol Bashota as well as with some friends from Drenica who we thought that were members of the central staff but turned out not to be later on. At that time we didn't have a consistent place where the central headquarters was stationed. Personally, for the first time I saw it in the number it existed in the -- 1998 [as interpreted]. At that time, you could contact the central staff, but in the capacity of a representative of the general staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to move now into the next month, that is June of 1998. We have heard and there really is no -- sorry, we're pausing for a minute, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I do apologise. There's a -- I'm looking at the wrong line. Yes, I see. Your Honour, apparently in - I'm obliged - in the line 20 on the screen that we're looking at at the moment, it should read "not existed -- in the 1998" -- in the December, I think, was the word or the month mentioned and it's not there. It's being confirmed. Yes, I'm much obliged. Perhaps that's another alteration that could be noted for the final version of this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, the question I was going to ask you moving into June is that we know that a representative of the general staff appeared --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wonder if that could be clarified with the witness because I didn't hear "December." So if December was said, it was not translated. We could go back and listen to the tape, but maybe it would be easier to clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I think you heard that.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did you say "December" or did you not?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that for the first time I saw the central staff, the general staff, in the beginning of December of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you very much. Again, I'll have another go at this question. The question I want to ask in relation to June 1998 is that we're all aware that in that month a member of the general staff made a statement on behalf of the KLA, and that that person, Jakup Krasniqi, paid a visit to Klecka. So I want to come on to that, if I may. Were you present in Klecka to meet Jakup Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you'll allow me, I think I left an opinion uncompleted, which I find very important in reference to the developments in Malisheve and my concerns about these developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I'll put that question on hold while you add your concerns.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Honoured Judges, the developments after the 29th of May and after Malisheve became a kind of a free territory without military activity by the KLA units, one of my concerns was the following. The capacity of the KLA to defend that region was insufficient. As I said, the -- that region became under the control of the KLA not as a result of the KLA activities. Secondly, the danger to which the citizens were exposed as well as the KLA members was great; we were in great danger. In case the Serb forces tried to deblock those roads in order to enter Malisheve, they could do so. I was sure that they could do so because I know that -- I knew that our forces were insufficient. On the other side, the newly created circumstances, for us everything was new and we were concerned because now it was not the same time as when we were a guerrilla unit. Now I'm speaking from my own experience. What a man can do most is to sacrifice himself and the consequences are on him. In order to attack a police patrol or a police station, we were the ones who were putting ourselves in danger. The others were not endangered. And that's why our activity in this direction was self-sacrificing one and everyone had their own responsibility, those who had voluntarily decided to join the KLA. Therefore, every activity that was carried out by the five of us, the results were affecting us, not someone else. As of now, we passed on to an entirely new situation. These new circumstances could put the civilian population into danger as well. It was quite normal that we would respond to an attack launched by the Serb forces, but our concern was whether we would be able to defend the citizens. And therefore, I think that there were some steps taken in euphoria without any prior preparations. The situation was no longer controlled by the general staff; it was out of control. It was gradually becoming an pan-popular [Realtime transcript read in error: "unpopular"] uprising. As we were acting in profound illegality, the KLA was not known, its strength was not known. And in a way, this was in our favour as to the Serb forces and the civilians themselves. It was easy when you contact a civilian, and if that civilian asks you whether you have sufficient forces to fight the Serb forces, you could easily say yes. If you were asked, do you have sufficient weaponry? It was easy to say yes. But after the 29th of May when thousands of young men and people knew what address to go to, those who wanted to join the KLA, and these places that they addressed themselves to, my answer to them was that for the time being we don't need new members. When there's a need, we will let you know. But later on, another group will -- would approach us. And then it was becoming obvious to them as well that we were -- we didn't have enough weapons. Those who had weapons were immediately engaged and became members of the KLA, and those who didn't were sent back. So those people who were sent back, they searched for their own ways to join. It was a time when everybody was engaging into finding a solution. Fortunately, my concerns, as perceived by the Serb forces, were wrong. And as time showed, this was because the Serbs did not intervene. The Serb forces did not intervene, and with this they helped the KLA to gain time in order to accommodate itself to the newly created circumstances. This is what I wanted to say. And I'm sorry I forgot your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think I have myself, but don't worry. I want with Their Honours permission to just correct something. Once again -- at page 30, line 9, it's at the top of the screen now: "It was gradually becoming an unpopular uprising." The words that I'd actually written down I think he said -- it was translated as a "pan-popular uprising," in other words across a country as a whole. I think that's what he said. Yes, Mr. Limaj, you heard what we just said. Did you say pan-popular?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that it began to have the signs of an all-popular uprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, right -- well, you've corrected it now. Thank you. Now, the question I was going to ask you concerns the month of June, the general staff, and a representative of the general staff who came to Klecka, Jakup Krasniqi. Now, first of all, did you meet Jakup Krasniqi in Klecka?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Was that his first visit there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was his first visit. If you want me to, I can explain how this visit happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One night before the arrival of Mr. Krasniqi in Klecka, Mr. Hashim Thaqi, Rexhep Selimi, and I think Sokol Bashota came to see me. They told me that they needed a place, a room, because on the following day the spokesperson of the KLA was going out in the public and we wanted to do this for the security and safety of Mr. Krasniqi and his family. They said they want to do it in Klecka so that the public opinion would not know from where Mr. Krasniqi was addressing them. They asked me to remove from the base those soldiers that I had there so that they could not witness and see the arrival of Mr. Krasniqi in that place -- as I was able to do that because I had enough place and space. On that night they brought a computer just for visual purposes, for television broadcast, and they brought a table. And on that night, we arranged the room so that it could look official according to those conditions that we had at that time. On the following day, Mr. Krasniqi came. Two journalists from the Albanian television had come before Mr. Krasniqi. Then Mr. Krasniqi came. He entered the room. We had a coffee, and on the spot Rexhep proposed that two KLA soldiers should stand on the sides of Mr. Krasniqi while he is reading his statement. This was an exclusive statement which was going out for the first time. And for the first time, the public opinion in the country and abroad would be able to see and get acquainted with a representative of the KLA with his full name and appearance. As we had removed the soldiers from there, as there was no one there except for myself and a relative, a close relative to Mr. Krasniqi. So we stood on each side of Mr. Krasniqi, and we were there during the time when the statement was given. After the statement was given, Mr. Krasniqi immediately left my base. Then Sokol Bashota told me that they had another base near the village of Klecka. Your Honours, there is a village which is called Divjake. It has no more than ten houses, and those who don't know that region, they take it for Klecka. They think it's Klecka because it's very close to Klecka and it's a mountainous region. That base was a KLA base from before, but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I didn't know that. The owner of that house was imprisoned at the same time with Demir and he was imprisoned with Demir because of his activity in the KLA. So they had started to use that house as a base, the representatives of the KLA, while passing from one region to another. He told me this for two reasons. one, for my soldiers in Klecka to be careful now that everyone knew who Jakup Krasniqi was. So for my soldiers in Klecke to be careful and guard that place and not tell other soldiers why they're guarding that place. So Mr. Krasniqi came frequently to that house and I went frequently to meet him in that place, maybe not on a daily basis but I surely went there once in two days. And depending on whether I had something to ask or if I had work to do, I would go on a daily basis. So whenever he was there, I would go and visit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if -- since you've mentioned that place, looking at the large-scale map, it does appear it is marked. Would you kindly go to the large-scale map which is folded over at the moment, and circle the village and the house where the ten houses is marked. I think it's to the north-east of Klecka.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village is here, however the houses are scattered and for someone who doesn't know the region, it is difficult to tell which are the houses of Klecka and which are those of Divjake. I forgot to mention the name of the owner of the house where Mr. Krasniqi was staying. If I'm not mistaken his name was Nezir Zogaj. And later on after November or December, the entire general staff was stationed there. So that place was a public knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just for the record, the map you're marking and have been marking so -- because there are three maps, it will be eventually, as I understand it DL4, so -- but I'm not going to exhibit it, with permission, for the moment until you continue marking anything else on that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, may I just --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to tell you that after giving his statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Right. Yes. Do continue.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He, Mr. Krasniqi, took the PC with him. So they took away the table and the computer to the place where they had taken it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, a further matter arising out of your earlier answers. When you said you might go -- when Mr. Krasniqi came you would go and see him quite often. It's an obvious question, but what would you go and see him about? Why were you going to see him when he was there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the developments I mentioned following the 29th of May in Malisheve, things had to be clarified. It was not sufficient to say, yes, we are working, things are getting well, we are working, and so on. Things which we have been doing so far. Now we had to be open, more transparent, more concrete. We needed to have available more accurate information as to what we should do from now then -- onwards. So I think that after a week following Mr. Krasniqi's public appearance, I went to him with three demands. First, I asked him to inform us - because in my view, he was the most competent person with which we could discuss issues directly. He could inform us about what we should do, what the plans of the headquarters were - we wanted to discuss whether taking control of Malisheve in the way I described was done in the knowledge -- with the knowledge of the headquarters, what would be done regarding the new organisation of the KLA. I was interested to know what the situation was, whether the headquarters had contacts with the political leadership or the political parties or class in Pristina. Because Mr. Krasniqi was one of the political activists, one of the personalities involved the political movement in Pristina I believed that he was the right person to give me an answer about that. The new circumstances, the demands we received on a daily basis from the citizens, made us seek solutions. I said earlier it is easy to make a decision to sacrifice yourself or to undertake actions which -- whose consequences or outcome affect only you personally. But when it comes to actions that may have an impact on a broader level, on a broad community, then the responsibility is greater. So in real terms, we were in a situation that we couldn't make any concrete decisions. I didn't know what we should do in the new circumstances. I didn't know whether the KLA was prepared for this new phase. In Malisheve, daily there were over 20.000 citizens coming. It was a small town. People came from other regions, as I said, from all over Kosova to see what was going on. And we at that time didn't have in place any civil structure that could control the life or organise a life of the people or could create the logistical base for the soldiers and for the population. So there should be some sort of coordination. And that situation, in my opinion, was unbearable. Therefore, I thought that the general headquarters should come out with a concrete plan of measures about what to do, what we were supposed to do in the new circumstances. And this was one of the topics that I discussed with Mr. Krasniqi at that time. And I may inform you, if you wish, about the replies of Mr. Krasniqi who shared his concerns with me. As to the contacts with the political people at that time, he told me that there are some contacts, even though there are difficulties. Pristina is creating problems for us, he told me, but we hope that we will find a common language. He told me also that we have greater hopes in the representatives of the KLA who had started to establish contact with a government in exile in order to coordinate operations and actions. With respect to the new circumstances created, Mr. Krasniqi told me that the general staff was unprepared for that situation. It didn't have the necessary structure to cope with them. Developments occurred too fast for them to cope with, that is the headquarters, that the way Malisheve was taken, he said, as I said earlier, this was a kind of replica action that went on and on and that the general staff couldn't control the situation. But he'd also told me that now that the population wants to join and seeks weapons, they were trying to find arms supplies, and leaving aside the question of the future organisation. The way he described the situation was that it was very difficult but that work was under way to find solutions for the new situation created. One of them, he said, was the development in Drenice where the operational zone was being consolidated with its command structure and then it would continue further on. Something similar was expected to have in Dukagjin and then in Pastrik. I think that the day I went to talk to Mr. Krasniqi, if I'm not mistaken it was the 22nd or the 23rd of June. That was for the first time that I received rules of work. I think it was on the 22nd of June, that was the first step undertaken by the headquarters -- the general headquarters which had begun to determine the objectives of the further organisation and consolidation of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned in that answer the emergence of operational zones, starting with Drenice. And in that answer, you went on to specify Pastrik. Now, so far as you're aware, when were the first moves to establishing the operational zone of Pastrik? When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This working meeting with Mr. Krasniqi occurred sometime, for this issue that I'm talking about, on the 20th. Then on the 22nd of June, I received that rules that I mentioned, that he offered me. It was in the beginning of July, I think, sometime -- it was the 5th, the 6th, or the 7th, I am not certain about, but it was in July. The first step was taken in this regard after we had talked with him. The general headquarters began to nominate the commanders of Pastrik operational zone -- commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And who were the commanders who were nominated by the general staff of that zone?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first commander appointed by the general staff for Pastrik zone was Muse Jashari in the beginning of July. Muse Jashari came from Adem Jashari's glorious Jashari family, our legendary commander's family. The general staff had decided that to appoint such a man enjoying great authority and having long experience in fighting, because he had been involved in fighting in the KLA for a long time by that time, that would be a solution that would be acceptable to all the units of the KLA, the units that operated in Malisheve, Suhareke, Rahovec, and Prizren municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did he have a deputy?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, that was the first step, the appointment of the commanders. Then he was left time, the commander, to consult various units and at the end come up with a proposal to the general staff for the zone command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: As far as you're concerned, were you given a role or an appointment or a command, as it were?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The appointment of Muse Jashari who came to Malisheve, that was an unknown terrain for him. When we talk about Suva Reka, Rahovec, and Prizren, in some villages there was public organisation in place and part of Prizren, but not in general. And it was difficult for the KLA units to communicate among themselves at that time. So at that time Jakup Krasniqi asked me to help Muse for his contacts in Malisheve. He asked not only me but also the commanders of other units in that area to help him to facilitate his work in order to consolidate a list of proposed candidates for the zone command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to see if it's possible, probably using one of the Prosecution maps. Would you be in a possible to delineate the area that you thought was covered by this operational zone in July 1998? Would you be able to do that with a circle, mark with a pen. I'll show you the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It's P1, map 6, please. Could it be put on the ELMO, please. It's the easiest one for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it intended that this be marked?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think there -- I've just realised there are spare copies of this sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I happen to have one myself which is -- it isn't marked. I don't know whether that's suitable, in fact. It's got a water mark at the top. If the witness could have the -- it is in fact an exact replica of this -- copy of this page, map 6, P1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I know you've seen this map, obviously, many times. If you could just take your time with a marker pen, so far as you're able, the zone as you understood it, the operational zone, in July 1998.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that the principle for dividing the operational zones was the territory falling under the municipalities; that was the simplest and uncomplicated division. So on the basis of the territories of the respective municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Would you just put it on the ELMO so we can see as you draw. It's a bit easier to follow that way, rather than just looking at it after you have done it. I'm sorry. You may need to sit sideways to do that.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I need to change this. [Interpretation] So as I explained to you, the principle, the underlining principle, was the division of the territories by the municipalities. This is the zone, the operational zone, of Pastrik. That is the border. That is the operational zone that was planned to be, that is, based on Drenice municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: That's the one outlined in red that you've just drawn. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Drenice Operational Zone more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Mansfield, there is a line drawn in blue. The area as I understand it, to the south-west of that line is the Pastrik zone. There is then a line in red, and the area to the north-west of that is the second zone. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That part is wrong because it belongs to the municipality of Fushe Kosova. This is the planned Nerodime operational zone. It includes the municipality of Malisheve, Rahovec, Suhareke, Prizren, Dragash. The Pastrik operational zone included what I mentioned. The Nerodime included Ferizaj and later some changes are made in the zones, Kacanik pass is transferred to Nerodime, even though the plan was to include them in the Karadak zone. But after the offensive of August, some changes occurred and Kacanik was left in the context of Nerodime operational zone and not that of Karadak, as the plan was initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to again -- to follow His Honour's lead, the area in black that you've just drawn was intended to be the Nerodime zone. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I know it's shooting forward a bit, but I will save having to get this out again. Using this same plan but a different marker pen, we know in August that there was a different organisational zone, the 121 Brigade. Could you for these purposes at this stage superimpose on this map the area of responsibility of that brigade, 121. Can you do it in a different colour.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After August, after the establishment of brigades and the summer offensive, we see changes which were brought about as a result of the changes in the terrain. The 121 Brigade is formed in the territory of the three operational zones at that time. It begins -- this is the asphalt road. From Orlat in this area, part of Orlat was under 121 Brigade zone. One was under 113 Brigade zone. Along this road, Orlat-Malisheve, always in the -- this part. This is a dividing line. It continues around Malisheve along the way, the road, the Malisheve, Dulje. Always if we go from Malisheve to Dulje it's on the left side, Your Honours. This is the border line of the brigade. In Dulje there is also the main road, Prizren-Prishtine. And if we go from Prizren to Prishtine, it falls on the left side. It continues on this line. Here it turns to Zborce, I think. It goes on to Vrshec, or Blinaje, Miletci [phoen], Mirene and turns and meets the Prishtine-Peja road. And it turns here downwards to -- towards Komorane, Lapusnik, and it meets the other line in Orlat. This is the territory that falls under the command of 121 Brigade, which was formed, as I said, in the territory of three operational zones -- intended zones that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I wonder, Your Honour, if this could become exhibited at this stage. I think in view of the other maps will be 4, 5, and 6, this should be DL7, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I suggest that we put them all in at this point --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- Mr. Mansfield. We're getting a bottleneck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So. So could it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have 4, 5, and 6 on the basis that if there is to be further marking by this witness it can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Could the ordinance survey map be DL4. This is the order in which they've been used. What's called the post-war route map, Kosovo, DL5; the political map, DL6; and this one, that is a version of -- copy of P1, map 6, that becomes DL7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Map number 1, which is the pre-war Serbian Ordinance Survey map of 1995 would be given Exhibit Number DL4; map number 2, which is the post-war political map of Kosovo dated 2000 will be given Exhibit Number DL5; map number 3 which is post-war routine map of Kosovo dated 2001 will be given Exhibit number DL6; and map number 6 from Prosecution Exhibit P1 which has been marked by the witness will be given exhibit DL 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Slight reversal of your order, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I don't think it's important. We can leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Can we go back to the position, Mr. Limaj, we were in. In other words, we were in June at the moment, taking it slightly out of order so we have the maps marked. This is after Krasniqi has paid the visit and so forth. What other developments in June so far as you are concerned and the KLA are concerned, what other things happened in June that you can recall of any significance?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, the meeting with Mr. Krasniqi came as a result of the concerns from what was seen in the terrain and what was going on on the terrain. The people began to come with the request to join the KLA. They wanted to get weapons and join the ranks, and they came in great numbers. I would like to say that these people were mainly young men. And just for your information, from 1991 there were whole generations of Albanian young men who did not complete military service. So Albanian youth between 1981 and 1991 had not completed the military service. They wanted to join just out of their free will to fight for their country. Just like us, they had no idea how to use weapons and how to act in those war circumstances. These were young men, 18, 19 years old, who unlike the older ones were not suitable to join the KLA. As I said, we were not prepared. We didn't know how to act with these people who wanted to join. And at that time while we were acting in illegality, I personally - because I always speak on my behalf - I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. thought that we were entering Kosova because Kosova needed people who were ready to sacrifice themselves and with this we could draw the attention of the international community that there is a need for solution here. However, the developments in June, they made us -- the necessity made us search for a solution in order to survive, because as you had launched a propaganda for KLA, now you could not say that I don't know what to say. So in Klecke there was an intention to set up a training centre because at that time I had established contacts with a reservist, an officer, as the reservist system existed from the Yugoslav Army, who knew military rules. He was an elderly person and was ready to assist with the training of young men who had no idea how to use weapons. Klecka was a suitable place for such a purpose. We started up with a group of 15 or 20 men to train these men. This officer was directly involved in the training, and at the same time this was a way to respond positively to the people because you could just not tell them all the, Go back, go back. So in a way we started a training, and depending on the situation some were trained for five days, some for six days. Young men completed a kind of a course, and then they were told that they have to go home and that they would be informed for their further engagement. So they went to the units that they wanted to join. Secondly, as Mr. Krasniqi told me, almost the entire general staff had engaged in procuring weapons because the question of weapons was the number one question. So they were all interested in getting as much weapons as possible and arming people who wanted to get armed. So those who came to us, we began to send them to Albania for weapons. And upon their return, they decided for themselves where they would get settled. Some would go to friends [Realtime transcript read in error: "France"], some to families. They decided for themselves where they were going to stay and settle down. So this is how things developed day by day. You should have in mind the situation how it was in that time, the concerns about the difficult situation at that time. For example, soldiers in Malisheve municipality, as they lacked weapons and did not have military barracks where they could stay. They all stayed in their own houses. A system of shifts was introduced. Some were serving in front line for eight hours and then resting for eight hours. So let's say someone who worked in a shop, he went on the front line and completed his shift for eight hours and then went back. And then he was replaced by another person who completed his shift for another eight hours and then went home. In concrete cases of danger, the issue of dislocation came into existence because you had to be able to dislocate those people in case of danger, but this was not possible. The only possible way for these people was for them to stay in houses and eat there. They couldn't stay anywhere else. So something had to be undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could I just interrupt. I'm sorry. There are a couple of transcription errors I think. The first one is right at the top at the moment. I think the witness said "the people who had weapons who joined were accepted immediately and sent to the units." We've just gone off the page. That was one thing. The second is still on the page, at line 6, page 45, "some may have gone to France." I think that would be wishful thinking, but again it's an error. So I make those two points so it's clear at this stage. I want to ask you a further question. You mentioned in the context of training an elderly gentleman.
