Who was the elderly gentleman who was employed for the purpose of training?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Ajet Kastrati. He was not employed but he was a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move further forward in time, and that is we know that at the end of July - we're now into July - you talked about getting various rules from Krasniqi and so on and the operational zone on the 5th, 6th, and 7th of July. The end of July, obviously there was, as we've heard, a very important battle on July the 26th. Now, so far as the month of July is concerned and June, did you during those two months have further occasions to go to Lapusnik for any reason?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Again, can you give us some idea of how often you went, how many times you may have gone in those two months.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to give a number because a number can be interpreted in different ways. I can say that I went there often. As you have said, I have gone 20 times. Maybe I have gone less than that or more than that, but what I can say is that I went there when I saw that there was a need for me to go there. Either on the way going to Drenica, both during July or June -- Now I just remembered an incident which is important and can be linked with what will be said. During that time for the first time I was able to see official officers, professional ones. It was a group of three or five officers -- maybe there were more of them, but personally I see three of them, officers who had completed military academy, who had come from abroad and joined the KLA. And with -- via the general staff, they were observing the terrain. And if I can say, they were, in a way, surveilling the terrain and every unit. Amongst these persons were Byslym Zyropi; the second person, who is a national martyr now, is Agim Qelaj. And the third, whose name unfortunately I don't remember at the moment, but his pseudonym was Hans because he came from Germany. I don't remember his name at the moment, but his name can be easily found. He fortunately is still alive. So these people came to us as well. They came to me at Klecka. They also visited different units and points in Lapusnik, Negrovce, Kishna Reka, they also went to Suhareke and Dukagjin area. They went to different villages in Drenica. Shortly they went to different points and places. What I wanted to say was this was the first time for us to see professional military officers, and this was something that we experienced for the first time and something that gave us hope for the future. We thought that with these people, initiatives will be taken and these initiatives will be taken by people specialised in these fields. We were very happy to see the presence of these officers. I know that Agim Qelaj from that small training centre that I mentioned, since Agim Qelaj was specialised in military training, he took three or four of my soldiers. He was inspired to create an intervention unit, so he took three or four soldiers from my unit and some soldiers from other units. This was by the end of June. So he prepared them, trained them, and sent them to Negrovce village, somewhere at the Vucjak gorge, there is a place between Negrovce and Turiqevc village, which is suitable for such activities. So this is how it developed. I know that we visited Lapusnik with them as well. I remember this moment when we went together to visit Lapusnik. They saw the place, they gave an idea or two to Isak or Ymer, whoever was there. I was on other occasions as well. Whenever I would go to Likovc, because I went there frequently in order to visit my friends not on duty or for specific tasks, I just wanted to see them as friends. So it was necessary to pass by Lapusnik in order to get to Likovc. Whoever wanted to go to Likovc had to pass through Lapusnik first, to stop there, have a coffee, discuss with someone, and this was a normal routine. So on my first visit -- during my visit, the first thing I would do is see Isak or Voglushi. On other occasions I've visited Lapusnik and other units as well on the way to Likovc, units when you pass by the road from Orlat that leads to Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some specific questions. Again, it's the period June to July. Firstly, during that time, did you participate in any way in the organisation or establishment of a prison camp in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This is absurd. I told you what our main problems and preoccupations were. It was impossible to imagine such a thing and to have to do with such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to ask you -- you've mentioned Isak Musliu. I want to ask you about the other defendant who sits with you here in The Hague, Mr. Bala. Before this case, had you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say that there is a difference between meeting and knowing someone. And after arriving here, Bala himself told me - because I didn't remember - he said that we met in 2001. He had come to me to ask for a favour for intervention at Pristina Hospital regarding his daughter. I had never known this person before coming to Lapusnik [as interpreted]. And whether I have met him, it is possible because I have met with thousands of soldiers. But for me, he was unfamiliar. And as for the meeting in 2001, this is what he told me; personally I did not remember it. After the war soldiers would come on daily basis to ask for favours, for assistance, Your Honours - this was very normal - so that they could integrate in the developments, in the post-war developments. So it is possible that this meeting happened, but for me it is an event that I cannot remember. This is something that Mr. Bala told me himself, that we've met in 2001, and it is possible. I didn't know this person before I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want -- with your help if it's possible, since you've indicated you've been to the Lapusnik area on a number of occasions, if you're able now with the assistance of an aerial photograph of Lapusnik to point out where you think you went in Lapusnik. It is, in fact, again Prosecution Exhibit 1, and it's image 8. If that could be -- I do not have a copy of that one -- that particular page, but if you could have a look at the exhibit, please. Image 8 is entitled "Aerial image of Lapusnik." And I think -- certainly these -- some of these have already been marked by other witnesses reasonable care so what I would like you to do - yes, we have it now on your monitors - is with the use of the indicator, the silver stick you've got there somewhere, the baton --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No, it's not here -- yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Do you have -- you don't actually write on it. No. All right. If you can just point -- we can see the road at the top which is the road Pristina in -- off to the right as you look at it and Peja off to the left as you look at it. That's the road at the top, to get your bearings. Now, looking at that, can you now remember by pointing to the areas where you think you went on the number of occasions that you went, and can you indicate what it was that you went to see or the person you went to see when you indicate an area.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as you might see for yourselves, this road here goes to this side; the other road goes to Likovc. This is the road that links the internal part -- the interior of Drenica with this part. So whoever had to go along this way. I have visited this group of houses here. I have had a coffee -- because there was a military unit of the village, of the neighbourhood. It had the name of the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm wondering if I can make a suggestion to assist here. We have extra copies of the map; however, we don't have them in the courtroom. Mr. Younis has some in his office. Perhaps the break could be taken a little early. We could provide an extra copy of the map and it could be marked for a clearer record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. In view of that, we'll break - it's only five minutes early - and resume at about quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: With Your Honours' permission, may I just clarify with the witness an answer that he gave. It's page 49, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, just before the break you were dealing with Mr. Bala and you made a distinction between meeting and knowing. And in that context you said, and we've had it checked, you'd never known Mr. Bala before coming to Lapusnik. Now, is that right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not right. I said I have never known him before coming here to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Right. Yes. I'm -- it's either been misheard or you misstated it. I don't go over that ground. Yes, thank you for that clarification. Do you now have a copy of image 8, Prosecution Exhibit 1? It should be on the ELMO. If it isn't, perhaps it could be put there -- right. Maybe it's mine. Sorry. Lucky I didn't mark it. Sorry. This is another copy of the image 8, which we all have in Prosecution Exhibit 1. Aerial image of Lapusnik. You had begun to look at this and you had already pointed to just below the main road Peja-Pristina to an area. And now perhaps with a marker pen you could go back to that area and circle it and indicate what -- perhaps put a number on it so we know from your evidence what the relevance of the area is. So perhaps we could start the process of where you went in this general vicinity, please.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have problems with maps. I have seen -- I have looked at it for a long time, actually, trying to remember some of the eventual visits I paid. Your Honours, here you can see there is a house. I remember that because that was a house of an old man, a pleasant old man I would say, who received us often. We had a good communication with him, and every time I went there I went to visit this sick old man. His name was Qerkin Sopi. If I'm not mistaken, his house must be somewhere in this area. Shall I circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, please circle it and please put a -- put a number 1 by that one so we know you're talking about the house of Mr. Sopi or the area where you think his house was. Sorry, I'm going to interrupt, if I may. In order -- if you can remember looking at this aerial map and all the difficulties, can you remember on the occasions you went to visit him how you got there, in other words the route or the road or the track you used to get to his house?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you just indicate it, please.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this is the entrance, if I might say so. It goes on along this direction, if I am not wrong. It is an narrow road. It continues along this line here. Here, as you can see. Here you could take either this direction and come here or this other direction, even though it was a longer path, the second one. And you could reach this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this other direction that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Now, I want to ask you about any other places that you can remember visiting in this vicinity.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have visited other houses in some instances. We might have stopped somewhere where there have been soldiers or some civilian might have invited us for a coffee, but these were impromptu visits. Another one I remember was here in the vicinity of Qerkini's. It is next to his home, more or less here. I remember because I think it was used as an outpatient clinic, a sort of outpatient clinic. I remember well that it had a yard, a garden surrounded by vineyards. And I know because it was summer and we drank the coffee outside in the garden with the owner who had this clinic in his house. Ferat Sopi I think was his name. It was here, somewhere here. Isak was also somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you mark that one with a 2. You've put 1 I think on the first one. That's it.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think here in this area, Isak used to sleep here close to this house. So when I went there, I met Isak here at the clinic, sometimes as Qerkini's. We might have eaten together. I told you that I had a good relationship with this old man. He was a former political prisoner. He was very pleasant to talk with. And I know that he was semi-paralyzed. But strangely, he seemed to recover after the developments that I mentioned about the KLA. It was inexplicable, his recovery. So every time I went there, I met him. Then in the course of our conversation, I found out that he knew my uncle. So sometimes, as I said, we ate together, drank coffee. It was a pleasure that I went there. But I might have visited other houses as well. I stopped here to drink a coffee -- to have a coffee, here, here; there were some civilians that happened to pass by and they offered coffee. They invited you to lunch -- not only me myself but also other soldiers. We might have stopped at their homes, might have drunk a glass of water, eaten lunch. So all these are things we may have done. I can't rule them out. But the same was true of the other part, because as I'm describing it is a small neighbourhood in Lapusnik. Lapusnik is a wide area. There was a friend of mine, for example, a soldier when I was a soldier myself for those ten days, and I stayed at his -- I stopped at his home, too, and had a coffee with him when I passed on to the villages of Drenice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you ask you a specific matter, namely: Are you in a position to indicate, if you knew, where the particular units or points were in this area? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try. Celiku 3 unit was positioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you put a circle as before?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have made some mistakes. It's an approximate location. One position was here, another might have been here, another one here. Please take it approximately because I can't be exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another here. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 -- 5 positions. The last one I think was somewhere here, not here but here. So these were the points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I just want to ask you this: Did you have any say in where the points where from time to time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly where the positions were. If I went to some military positions, I went here to -- from this house here, here. In the vicinity of the house where I had stopped. I may err to tell the exact position of it, but I know there were five. Other units were positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes -- sorry, it's probably my mistake in being translated. I was asking whether you in fact yourself had made decisions about where points should be in this area.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, before we leave this aerial image, are there any other features here that you recall, any houses, places that you went?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to tell you that here in this place it is outside the zone, actually somewhere here. There is the Kizhareke village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It was off the monitor, so we didn't see. Can you just point it again. Sorry about that. It has to be moved slightly so we can see where you're pointing.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may make some mistakes because it's outside the focus of this map. It's somewhere here I think. This is the Kizhareke village. There was a unit positioned here. Here there was another unit, a neighbourhood unit that I mentioned earlier. I don't think it had a name. The villagers of that neighbourhood organised themselves, purchased arms, wanted to defend their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you just put a circle where you last mentioned the unit, and I think we're up to 3. If you could number that one 3. The other ones were points, so I wouldn't ask you to number.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was -- number 4 was here, where the road turns here. Here there -- at this place there were soldiers who control the entries and exits. I think it was part of that unit. It was a joint unit made up of villagers. I'm repeating it, that these were villagers who organised themselves, purchased their own weapons, and wanted to protect their homes because there were some acts of burglary committed, since most of the population, civilian population, had left. So a small number remained. And then there are other units which I cannot see in this part of the map. On the other part of the Lapusnik gorge, along all the valley, like the Pellumbi, Lumi, Guri, Murrizi, Ferra, the names of various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think that will do for the aerial, that you indicated it doesn't cover all the units you knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could that become -- we're up to 8 I think. Could this become this marked version DL8, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Map number 8 will be given Defence Exhibit DL8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to stress, Your Honours, that I may have visited other homes, but in my memory they didn't constitute any special occurrence. It was part of our daily life because we did eat and sleep at other people's homes; that was part of our daily living. So I can't rule out the possibility, as I said, of visiting other homes. But if it happened that I visited a single home twice or three times, that I certainly remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you, since we're dealing obviously with Lapusnik --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I forgot something. Besides here, now I remember, I was -- I visited -- not visited but I ate with some soldiers in a kitchen here, in a kitchen which was situated I think here, if I am not mistaken; here in this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you circle where you think it was, the kitchen, and put a number by that. We may be up to 4 by now.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: 5, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately here. I know that I have been there. There were 10, 12 soldiers. We went to have lunch together. It was an improvised, a makeshift kitchen, but they referred to it as a kitchen. I think it was after the battle of the 17th of May that we ate together with these soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to come to events at the end of July, in other words what has been known as the battle for Lapusnik, July the 26th. Did you participate in fighting on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lawyer, I would give you an answer about Lapusnik if you ask me about Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I have decided that, this case being a very important case for me, I want to tell before this Honourable Trial Chamber the truth, because I've been faced with -- for three years with a number of allegations and I want to tell the truth. So whenever and wherever you see something that you need to ask me about, please do so so that I can present to you my views before this Honourable Trial Chamber. Allow me, even if it takes too long, for me to explain the details. Allow me to tell whatever I know about that part of my life, what I have witnessed. I'm telling you that I want you to ask me about Rahovec because there is a very controversial issue. There have been many slanders, many allegations which have entailed sometimes my name. And I want to make some things clear, even though maybe it's not directly linked -- related to the case, but for me it is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes -- sorry, I'm looking at the clock and other things that have to be fitted in today if I can, so that is why I jump to the 26th and Lapusnik at the moment, and we're dealing with Lapusnik at the moment. Were you involved in fighting on the 26th of July? And then I'll come back to Rahovec, obviously.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not involved. I was involved in the second part of the first day, that is in the afternoon of the 25th. After 3.00 in the afternoon, I went there. Fighting was very severe. I couldn't go where I wanted to go, and there was a friend with me. I lost consciousness. I have health problems and there I had the same fit I had in Rahovec. On the 25th in the afternoon I went to take part in the fighting, but I couldn't go to the front line, couldn't penetrate. I had this fit, this loss of consciousness, and then afterwards I saw myself in Klecke where the soldiers had returned me. But on the 26th, I didn't go. There was no need for us to go there because at 10.00 in the morning the Lapusnik gorge fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, again I'm a question because of the context we're dealing with. I will come back to Rahovec; don't worry. I want to ask you whether at this time, that is on the -- thereabouts the 26th of July, you were in the Berisa Mountains, either on a tractor or off a tractor or with other soldiers in the circumstances where it is alleged prisoners from Lapusnik were being marched, effectively, in the end, to their death. Were you in the Berisa Mountains on such an occasion?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was sick at the time. But even if I were healthy, okay, it would be illogical for me to go from Berisa to Lapusnik because at that time Serbian shelling was very severe. We had problems even in Klecke, let alone to think of going to that place which was completely bare -- it is -- there are no trees. It's under constant fire from the Serbian forces. If you look at this map, this part of the map, this was proven also by the soldiers who were there, eyewitnesses. The Serbian tanks were stationed here, so we were under their full fire. Everything was -- any movement was impossible. As I told you, on the 25th I had a health problem, the same I had in Rahovec before. It was at 12.00 I think one of the soldiers came and told me that Lapusnik had fallen, Lapusnik gorge had fallen. So the first thing that came to my mind, the first concern for me was Malisheve because the falling of Lapusnik gorge meant that the Serbian forces would head for Malisheve, where there were about 100.000 people sheltered there coming from various areas. So Malisheve was overpopulated at that time. And my family, too, was among the residents, even though for me my family was -- mattered as much as the other families did. I may be wrong, but it was either 1.00 or 2.00. I tried to pull myself together and got up together with two soldiers. And we went with my nephew as well, Naser Sabit. We got in a car and went -- drove to Novoselle, as the map says, from Novoselle to Terpeze, from Terpeze along the asphalt road we went directly to Malisheve to inform the people to flee Malisheve gradually, to warn them that the Serbian forces might shell Malisheve, for them to find shelters elsewhere. Because usually from previous experiences, the Serbian forces were indiscriminate in their attacks in the -- in their treatment of the civilian population in the zones which had been under the control of the KLA. So we wanted the civilian population to find shelter, as I said, elsewhere. And so from Malisheve, the -- there were the shops and the coffees were full of food supplies. The people didn't know what to do with the supplies, with the people -- they were hoping that the Serbian forces might not come there. So we told them to get with them whatever they could and leave because the Serbian forces were on the way. I remember that in a store I got about 15 kilogrammes of coffee, which one of the salesmen gave to me on the road to Banje. So this I want to say that people began to get whatever they could from the food provisions. This was a good opportunity for people who were engaged in trade, because this place was full of refugees. That's why I'm saying that the stores were full of food supplies. And from there I went to Banje, to my native village. I talked with my family. I told them that they had to leave, because after Malisheve fell I knew that the other villages would soon fall. And then I went -- continued to inform the villagers, the inhabitants of other villages in Bellanice, Temeqine. We spread the word all over these places. Then we returned in the direction of Senik. From Senik in the direction of Lladrovc, telling everyone we met and saw to take to the mountains of Klecke, to take to the Klecke valley. Some went to Pagarushe. When I returned to Terpeze, it was late afternoon. Those soldiers who had withdrawn from the Lapusnik gorge, a large number of them were in Terpeze. During the time we had travelled from Malisheve, Banje, Terpeze, until we returned to Terpeze, the population, the civilian population, had taken the opposite direction and were coming in the direction of Terpeze. The road was full of tractors, lorries, trucks, whatever means the people had. So when the soldiers informed me of what had happened, we tried with the soldiers who were there, the others who came from Klecke, to form a front line in Terpeze, if for nothing, at least to delay the entry of the Serbian forces into Malisheve, to enable the civilian population to leave. And, on the other hand, to put up a defence line in Terpeze that if they attempted to enter Malisheve in the direction of Terpeze, we could hold them there, to prevent them from entering Klecke. So I want to say that all these movements, all these things I did without leaving the car, because I felt very weak after what had happened and after the intensive week I had passed. I think it was 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening I returned from Terpeze to Klecke. From Terpeze to Klecke at that time it took normally five hours to manage to penetrate into Klecke because of the very heavy traffic that I told you. The civilian population were using everything they could, and there was no other way for us to enter other than that road. So in the evening we managed to return to Klecke. And at 10.00, everything was over, as the eyewitnesses to the event say. That is a truth of that day. And in the evening, Isak came around 8.00. We didn't have information as to what the casualties were, who was dead, who was injured. He told us that Ymer was killed there, that -- we sat down and talked. Even though we were very tired, we talked with Isak and the others about what to do in these circumstances. We discussed about the soldiers who were there, those who were in Terpeze and in other places because as a result of that offensive, the soldiers spread out in many areas. So we tried to put up, as I said, a defence line and set up some observation points to survey the Serbian forces because we didn't know what their plans were, what they would do on the next day. We were worried because there were about 50.000 people scattered all over these mountains and hills and we had no idea whatsoever what might happen to them if the Serbian forces tried to penetrate into the hinterland of Terpeze, Lladrovc on the one hand and -- as I said, we had no idea what might happen. We were under extraordinary pressure. This is how events happened on the 26th, the way I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, before I move on to what you did with the people who were displaced, the refugees, I want to go back a fraction. You mentioned in that answer that it was at the end of a very intensive week and you were, yourself, very weak. And that, I suggest, takes us back to Rahovec and matters that had happened just before Lapusnik. So would you kindly now indicate what had been happening there before events erupted at Lapusnik. [Lladroc]?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a consequence of the developments in Malisheve. A copy of a previous situation. And people behaved the same way other people in other areas behaved. I forgot to mention an incident. Sometime in the beginning of July, the General Staff appointed civilian administrators for the municipality of Malisheve. I think this was a first appointment after the conversations I had with Jakup Krasniqi, and I'm sure that Jakup had conversations with others as well. And I think it was in this time that the General Staff appointed a civilian directorate in order to cope with the entire civilian population in Malisheve at that time. Gani Krasniqi was appointed chief of this civilian directorate. In the beginning of July he invited me to go down from Klecka because Malisheve was now a centre and to set up an office or a place in Malisheve and then designate the tasks that we were going to deal with. I did not accept this offer to leave Klecka and go to Malisheve for the reasons that I mentioned earlier. I didn't want to take up such a responsibility. And simply, as I said, Malisheve was not our result [as interpreted]. On the one hand I thought that if I went there, the General Staff had to make an appointment to see what I was going to do there. So maybe it's in the interest of this Chamber to know this fact. On the 17th of July, this is a first time after all that time while I was in Switzerland and in Kosova, this is a first time I decided to spend a night with my family. So throughout this time -- throughout this time in Kosova, this is the first time I decided to spend a night in my own house, because up to that time I had never gone to spend a night with my family. I had gone to visit them for an hour or two or have a lunch, but I had never slept in my house. It was around 11.30 p.m. I went from Klecka through Novoselle or Fshati i Ri but I'm using the toponym Novoselle because that's how it is marked on the map. When I arrived at the Malisheve crossroads, there is a place that divides a road from Dulje from one side to and the other side to Rahovec. There I saw a group of people and two soldiers. I stopped the vehicle. I was alone and I asked these people what were the news because it was 11.30. You could see that that was something extraordinary. There was some women and men and some soldiers speaking with them. I stopped the car to see what was going on. The soldiers told me that according to those civilians, there was fighting going on in Rahovec. And they for themselves were not sure whether that was true, but what they told me was that according to those civilians there was fighting going on in Rahovec and that a group of soldiers from Malisheve have gone to Rahovec for assistance and in order to find out what was going on there. As I felt this personal responsibility and I was not in peace with myself, I didn't want to go to my family without knowing what was going on. I could have done so, although nothing was at the time regulated by regulations, military regulations. Everything depended on your own decision. I set off in the direction of Rahovec. It was something extraordinary. It was something unexpected, these fightings at Rahovec. At the entrance of Rahovec -- Your Honours, I think there was a recording [as interpreted] that could best describe the city of Rahovec. At the entrance of Rahovec there are two roads, one going inside the city and one going around the city. I would like to tell you that I had never gone to that city before. Although it is close to Malisheve, I had nothing to do there. I had no family relations or a reason to go and visit this city. So when I went at the Rahovec crossroads, there I met soldiers from Rahovec. I asked them what was going on. They told me that there was combat going on inside the city. After this, I asked them about the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. soldiers from Malisheve that those soldiers before told me. They told me that these soldiers from Malisheve were directed to the entrance of Rahovec from Prizren side. I went towards this direction. At that time to enter Rahovec was not something that you could easily do. Only those who knew the terrain could do that. So I went straight to these soldiers from Malisheve. I saw these soldiers -- there's another road that divides the road that goes inside the city and the one that goes around the city. So these soldiers were there in the same way that the soldier from Rahovec had left them. I asked them, Why did you come here? Who told you to come here? And one of the soldiers asked me back, Why did you come here? And I said to him, Well, I heard about the combat. And he said, Well, that's what we heard, but there's nobody who can direct us where to go, what to do. And I said to them, Let's go away from this road. Because the Serbs were positioned at a place from where -- the place where we were was quite visible. And shortly after, Serb shells fell on that location and we -- if we stayed there for another second, I'm sure that there would have been casualties amongst us. I sent one of the soldiers to the entrance of Rahovec and meet [as interpreted] one of the leaders or one of the people from that place and ask him what was going on. A soldier came and he said to me, Well, no one from the leaders was there. And then I asked, Who gave the order? How come this fighting in Rahovec happened? And according to him, what he told me with you, several soldiers went to their homes in the city in order to visit their families, and that they were discovered by these Serb forces. The Serb forces went to arrest them. They resisted the arrest, and that's how the attack began. And after that incident, the soldiers who were positioned - because there were positioned units at the entrance of Rahovec, around Rahovec - and all these soldiers who were positioned and who were guarding the Rahovec-Malisheve road, when they heard the shooting they thought that their friends were getting killed, the families of their friends were getting killed and they all entered Rahovec. So whoever entered Rahovec at that time had no idea of what was going on. They were all entering Rahovec in order to help someone else. So I consulted the other 12 soldiers and decided that the best way we could help was to block the road and build up a defence line at the entrance of Rahovec. And I requested from some families at the entrance of Rahovec that they gave me some working equipment so that we could open up defence positions. I was sure that the Serb forces were not going to tolerate the situation as they tolerated the situation in Malisheve. I was sure that they were going to act. So at least I thought that it was good for us to create -- to establish a defence line that would direct the people who were withdrawing from the city. So we started opening up -- digging up trenches. So it took us some time to find the equipment. And at around 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning, we started digging up the trenches. And the first part of the next day, the 18th, at around 8.00 in the morning, I left that place, I left those young men, and went up thinking that I would be able to find someone who will be able to give me an answer about what was going on. And on that occasion, I met with Agim Qelaj and with Rexhep Selimi and Muse Jashari who had arrived there an hour earlier at the entrance of Rahovec. I can say that it was in a stressed way, in a nervous way that I asked which was that person? Who was that person, that organ, that body who gave the order to enter Rahovec? And at that time, the representatives of the General Staff, Rexhep Selimi, and Byslym Zyropi and Musa, they told me that they heard for the first time about the events in Rahovec this morning, at 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning. And in a hurry they came in order to see what was the situation and to find the way that would take us out from the position that the KLA was in and to avoid the danger to which the population was exposed. And the General Staff, Byslym Zyropi and Sokol Bashota, they decided that Agim Qelaj should become an operations commander for Rahovec and Agim became kind of a coordination point for all those that were there. So I informed them on this occasion that I had started to set up a defence line, a block, and I went back and I stayed there for the entire day and the entire night without any sleep. Maybe it would be appropriate to mention another detail. Sometime at around 4.00 a.m. I walked up a hill which is in the line with the positions that we had set up. And I wanted to light to cigarette, and I nearly fell asleep on the back of this soldier. And both myself and this soldier had turned our backs to Serb snipers who were at 100 or 200 metres from us. Both of us, we didn't know the terrain, but fortunately I think they were getting ready for the operation and they didn't want us to find out about their positions. And that's why we managed to survive. I slept for an hour, an hour and a half, then I went down to the point, to that front line that we had established. One of the inhabitants of the houses in the vicinity happened to be there, and I asked him for a coffee. He gave me a coffee. And after I had the coffee, I think it was half an hour after that, I didn't know anything about myself anymore. In fact, I had the coffee and then went to Agim and reported to him about the situation down there. And then I fainted. And in fact this person saved my life. Some of the soldiers took me to the clinic. There was a makeshift hospital in Gajrak, Malisheve municipality, and the doctors checked me up. This was how it happened in Rahovec. And if there is a mark about this period regarding the KLA, I think it's -- if there is a black stain, it's this because nobody knows how things really developed. This is one of the reasons I wanted to mention this, because I know this incident as a black stain that made the KLA pay a high price, both in casualties in its ranks and in -- and waivered people's confidence. Rahovec states or purely mirrors the way the KLA organised -- was organised at that time. It's a concrete example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want in the remaining time tonight in fact to deal with another what might be regarded as a black stain, since you've used that term, and that is the question -- the topic of collaborators. Did you have, yourself personally, a view about elaborators [sic]. Did you make distinctions and what were they?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like the others, I too had my views about them. In the case of the KLA, the communiques issued, most of them actually, issued by the KLA before the frontal attack, before the events followed in the summer of 1998 for them, collaborators were those people who were actively inspectors in the UDB or in the police, people directly involved in operations involving murders, assassination attempts, offences, or ransacking or searches, violation operation, imprisonment of people, continuous, persistent operations. That was the category that was seen as the Serb police by us, that is people who had exerted violence in the same way as the Serbs. In some cases, the collaborators who are inspectors, as I said, have led massacres perpetrated in Likoshan, Prekaz and Qirez, and in other places. There are some instances when those collaborators have led and staged ambushes against the KLA, like the case of Zahir Bajaziti was or Elmoz Hoxha, or Zejnullah. I don't remember his last name at this moment. Three killed soldiers. Or Rexhep Bislimi or the murder of Afrim Zhitija, Nuri Berisha. So these were people who were continuously involved in such operations, and these were looked upon as collaborators by the KLA. If in this Trial Chamber it has been said that a collaborator who was someone who had relations with the Serbs, who has cut wood or sold things to them. I am giving you an example. In Malisheve there were at least 500 private firms or companies who -- which had exclusive business relationship with other Serb cities and firms because you can imagine that we were entirely isolated. We could either trade with Macedonia or with Serbia. If we had some business with Macedonian firms, we had to pay taxes and it was very unfavourable for the citizens, so they didn't want to pay taxes. So the entire business activity was developed within the country, that is between us and Serbia, Serbian cities. And you won't find a single case. I'm talking about my own region, but I'm sure that this has happened everywhere. If someone has been taken -- expropriated of his cafe, his other restaurant, or whatever establishment he might have had, he is maltreated in prison, you won't find a single case. On the contrary, you'll see that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please ask the witness to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: In the last half an hour you have speeded up considerably. I wonder if it is possible in the embers in the day, if you could slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm under your pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I'm trying to tell you what I think is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just -- I'm going to pause for a moment just to catch your breath, as it were, and also the interpreters. You -- in that last answer you've made a distinction between those collaborators who in fact have caused deaths and collaborators in the sense that the Chamber's heard, people who might do business with Serbs. Now, taking those two categories for a moment. Do the two categories attract a different kind of treatment or the same treatment or what? And what is the treatment?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to give you my personal example, and you may give it your weight. It has been said here that someone who has worked as a forest ranger has been killed just because he had relations with Serbian people and he has been considered a collaborator. I'm telling you that my own father worked until 1998/1999 - he interrupted his activity when the war broke out - he has worked all along with Serbian colleagues. If we go by this logic, then how can that my own father has been working all the time with them? So it has got nothing to do with the truth. I am telling you again that it may have happened that some murders have been committed out of personal motives, out of personal revenge. This is another category. But to try to attribute to KLA this, the fact that all those who were working and collaborating with the Serbs were collaborators, then in this case we should have killed 90 per cent of the Albanians. Even though we were against the regime, we were obliged to communicate with the Serbs in all walks of life. So people had to live and they had to interrelate with one another. I lived in Pristina. On the same floor that I lived -- on the next floor where I lived, there was a Serb family and we used to greet each other every time we saw each other. But because I greeted them, I didn't -- doesn't mean that I was a supporter of Milosevic. I know -- I'm sure that they knew about my beliefs, my conviction that Kosova should be a state in itself, an independent state. And time has shown that right was on our side because it was those -- the Serbs themselves that overthrew Milosevic. I think that the tendency to mix up these elements and to tag such people as collaborators, this is groundless, this is not true. Malisheve, I mentioned the firms that are in Malisheve, but all over Kosova, there are hundreds of thousands of such firms and companies. You can find businessmen in Kosova who were directly working in cooperation with the criminal structures of Milosevic, who have made material gains out of this cooperation. They have evaded taxes, to give them money to bribe the state officials of Serbia. Our Albanian firms have cooperated with such businesses, and they have become very powerful today out of their cooperation with Milosevic's son or other such structures. But for me, this was not important. For me, it was important to harm the state -- the budget of Serbia. Now these people have their own businesses, their own economy, they are rehabilitated now. It is in the interests of the new institutions of Kosova to look into the origin of such people assets and wealth, but this is up to the institutions in Kosova. But the fact is that people got rich after the 1990s. Before that, they didn't have anything. You know that there are hotels and other businesses. And now, as you might see, their businesses are being legalised, Your Honours. I hope that the institutions of Kosova will at some point in future look into the origin of such wealth. I told this just to illustrate the level of cooperation among the -- between the Albanians and the Serbs because there was no way out for Albanians than to cooperate with the Serbs. How could we tell an establishment, an enterprise, not to cooperate with Serbia, not to bring cement, bricks, whatever, construction materials were needed. How could the houses be built if they were not allowed to do that? We couldn't tell an enterprise not to import -- not to bring sugar, flour, whatever, because we didn't have our own produce. It is illogical I think to look at such people in this way. I am still saying that the category of collaborators for me personally, and I think this was a prevailing concept in the KLA, were those people were engaged directly in criminal activities or operations, and I can give you examples of such people. In this case, I have learned many truths that I otherwise would not have learned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Mansfield, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I was just going to stop you in case you were going to give a list of examples. Others can ask you if they need it. I was going to ask you this question. In view of what you have said today. It's a hypothetical question, but it must be put to you. If during the months of May, June, and July 1998 it had been brought to your attention that there was a prison camp in which people who had had relations with the Serbs or had thought to have had relations with the Serbs were being seriously maltreated, what would you have done about it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have immediately reported this to the headquarters, to the leading bodies, to find out whether they knew, or at least to inform them, to alert them about that. Otherwise, I would not consider myself a member of the KLA. It would be suicidal to the KLA itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Besides reporting it, would you have done anything else?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I could have done something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I told you about the organisational level and the possibilities we had to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's slightly early, but the next topic will take rather longer than five minutes. May I assure the Tribunal we -- the topics I have left to cover will be finished well within the time tomorrow. So I apologise it's taken a little bit longer. May I also indicate when the witness mentioned a recording, I think he meant a film, if I eve got this right, and we would ask permission at some stage tomorrow that the film is shown. It's already on the list of exhibits. The Prosecution are aware of it. It's various shots of Kosovo, and in particular places that the witness has mentioned in his evidence. And the idea would be, subject to your approval -- it takes 30 minutes to show it, that he narrates the places that are on the film, and it's almost a substitute for the Court having a view, if I may put it that way. Those are the remaining matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, one concern I have from the comment you've just made, I think there was an estimate of three days made in respect of this witness. That should have been not only for examination-in-chief but all stages of examination and cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm thinking rapidly. I thought we'd made an estimate of four days altogether, in other words two in-chief and two for cross-examination. I think that was the original estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The one I have seen is three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, well I'm sorry -- someone to my right is admitting it is his mistake. It will not affect the overall structure. I had allowed two days. I am overrunning, I admit that. But it was never thought that we would get the whole of the cross-examination plus the examination-in-chief in three days. I don't think that was anticipated and I apologise if you have been misled. And Mr. Churcher, the next witness, has been asked to come -- to be ready for Tuesday, but I appreciate the Prosecution may not be finished by then, but it's certainly within our time scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If it comes to it, if -- for example, I can deal with the film in other ways. It doesn't necessarily have to be shown as part of his evidence. It's just that he knows the places and that would be sensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point is to ensure that the time estimates are recognised as covering the whole of the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or else we will creep out to double what is presently estimated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. May I assure you what we've done overnight - I don't know whether Mr. Whiting has been told and if he hasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He's now being told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: We have attempted to say straightaway -- we had a conference last night about these matters. The witnesses that we are definitely calling over the next two weeks, and by implication some of the witnesses on the list are already being dropped off, but effectively, a final decision cannot be taken while the defendant is giving his evidence. But we are working very hard -- I can assure Your Honour that there will be a much reduced list in his case. And we're not at the moment concerned that our case will -- in fact, I estimate three and a half weeks, maximum, for our case, even at the present rate that we're going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will suggest we should adjourn now before you have any change of heart, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of May, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
